questions.question:
Match List - I with List - II.

 
 

 List - I
 List - II
 
 
 
 

 A. Q theory
 I. Unemployment and inflation
 
 

 B. Phillips curve
 II. Unemployment and output
 
 

 C. Okun’s Law
 III. Investment
 
 

 D. Liquidity trap
 IV. Demand for money and interest rate
 
 

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
**The correct answer is: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

__
 
• **Q Theory (A-III):**

 
 
• The Q theory, or Tobin's Q theory, relates investment decisions to the market valuation of a firm. It posits that firms will increase investment when the market value of their existing assets exceeds the replacement cost of those assets.
 
• In simpler terms, when the Q ratio (market value/replacement cost) is greater than 1, investment is attractive because the market values the firm's assets highly.
 
 
 
• **Phillips Curve (B-I):**
 
 
• The Phillips curve shows an inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation in the short run.
 
• As unemployment decreases, inflation tends to rise because of increased spending and demand in the economy. Conversely, higher unemployment usually leads to lower inflation rates.
 
• This concept is central to understanding short-term trade-offs in macroeconomic policy.
 
 
 
• **Okun’s Law (C-II):**
 
 
• Okun’s Law describes the relationship between unemployment and output (GDP). It indicates that for every 1% increase in unemployment, a country’s GDP will be an estimated 2% lower than its potential output.
 
• This empirical observation highlights the cost of unemployment in terms of lost economic productivity.
 
 
 
• **Liquidity Trap (D-IV):**
 
 
• The liquidity trap occurs when interest rates are so low that monetary policy becomes ineffective. In this situation, people prefer to hold cash rather than invest in bonds or other financial instruments.
 
• The demand for money becomes perfectly elastic with respect to the interest rate, rendering traditional monetary policy tools (like lowering interest rates) ineffective in stimulating the economy.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Why other options are incorrect:**

 
 
• Options that mismatched the relationships between List I and List II are incorrect because they fail to correctly link the economic theories or concepts to their respective phenomena.
 
• For example, associating the Phillips Curve with output or investment (instead of unemployment and inflation) would be incorrect because the Phillips Curve is explicitly about the trade-off between unemployment and inflation.
 
• Similarly, linking Q Theory to unemployment would be inaccurate as Q Theory deals with investment decisions driven by market valuation.
 
• Okun's Law, which focuses on unemployment and GDP output, cannot be matched with other variables like inflation or investment.
 
• The liquidity trap is specifically associated with the relationship between money demand and interest rates, not with variables like unemployment or investment.
 
 
 
• **Practical Applications:**
 
 
• Understanding the Phillips Curve is crucial for policymakers to balance unemployment and inflation through fiscal and monetary policies.
 
• Okun’s Law helps in estimating the impact of unemployment on economic growth, assisting in GDP forecasting.
 
• The Q theory provides insights into corporate investment behavior, which is critical for financial markets and economic planning.
 
• Recognizing a liquidity trap helps central banks design alternative tools, such as quantitative easing, when traditional interest rate adjustments are ineffective.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The Q theory was introduced by James Tobin, a Nobel laureate economist, to explain investment behavior.
 
• The Phillips Curve was first observed by economist A.W. Phillips in 1958 based on data from the UK economy.
 
• Okun’s Law is named after economist Arthur Okun, who first presented this relationship in the 1960s.
 
• The concept of a liquidity trap was popularized by John Maynard Keynes during the Great Depression.

questions.question: According to the POCSO Act, what is the minimum punishment for a person who fails to report an offense under POCSO?

options.text: Imprisonment up to 1 year ​and/or with a fine.
Imprisonment up to 6 months and/or with a fine.
Imprisonment up to 2 years and/or with a fine.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is** Option 2**

**An offense** can be reported after it has occurred, or even before it has occurred, if there is fear that such a crime may occur.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Any person can report an offense under POCSO.
 
• The child facing or fearing such abuse can also report the crime directly. What is important is the crime MUST BE REPORTED.
 
• If a person fails to report an offense under POCSO, the person can be punished with imprisonment of up to 6 months and/or with a fine.

**Hence, we can conclude that Imprisonment of up to 6 months and/or with a fine is the punishment for a person who fails to report an offense under POCSO.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**If a **person is in-charge of an institution and fails to report an offense under POCSO** **committed by a subordinate **(i.e. someone over whom the person has professional control), the person can be punished with imprisonment of up to 1 year and/or with a fine.

__
 
• The **Election of the President** is governed by **Article 54** of the Indian Constitution, not Article 53.
 
• Article 54 specifies the procedure for electing the President of India, which involves an **electoral college** comprising elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States.
 
• Article 53, on the other hand, deals with the **Executive power of the Union**, stating that the executive authority of the Union shall be vested in the President.
 
• The President's election process is conducted under strict guidelines laid down by the Constitution to ensure a fair and transparent procedure.
 
• The President serves as the **constitutional head** of the country and represents the unity and integrity of the nation.

 __
 
• **Article 59** deals with the conditions under which the President holds office.
 
• It specifies that the President cannot be a member of Parliament or any State Legislature and should not hold any other office of profit.
 
• The President is entitled to an official residence and other allowances during the term of office.
 
 
 
• **The President of India - Article 52**__
 __
 
• **Article 52** establishes the office of the President of India as the head of the State.
 
• The President serves as the **chief executive authority** and symbol of national unity.
 
• The article emphasizes that India shall have a President who exercises powers as per the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Term of office of the President - Article 56**__
 
 
• **Article 56** outlines the President's term of office, which is **five years** from the date of entering office.
 
• The President may resign before the term or be removed through impeachment as per the constitutional provisions.
 
• The article also allows for re-election of the President after the completion of the term.

questions.question: The Chagos Archipelago is located in which of the following oceans?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Indian Ocean**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Chagos Archipelago** is a group of islands located in the **Indian Ocean.**
 
• It is situated approximately **500 km south of the Maldives** and is part of the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT).
 
• The archipelago consists of **over 60 tropical islands** spread across seven atolls, forming one of the world's largest coral atolls.
 
• The largest island in the group is **Diego Garcia**, which is also home to a strategically important military base jointly operated by the **United States** and the **United Kingdom**.
 
• The Chagos Archipelago is known for its **rich biodiversity** and is a designated **marine protected area**, although its designation has been a topic of international dispute.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Geopolitical Importance of the Chagos Archipelago:**

 
 
• The Chagos Archipelago is a contentious territory, claimed by **Mauritius** as part of its sovereign territory. Mauritius has argued its claim in international forums, including the United Nations.
 
• In 2019, the **International Court of Justice (ICJ)** issued an advisory opinion stating that the United Kingdom's administration of the islands is unlawful and that they should be returned to Mauritius.
 
• The archipelago's Diego Garcia military base plays a critical role in the geopolitical strategies of the **United States** and **United Kingdom**, especially in the Indian Ocean region.
 
 
 
• **Biodiversity and Environmental Significance:**
 
 
• The Chagos Archipelago is home to one of the world's largest **marine protected areas**, covering over **640,000 square kilometers**.
 
• The region is rich in **marine biodiversity**, including coral reefs, fish species, and other marine life, making it a critical area for global conservation efforts.
 
• It also serves as a nesting ground for **sea turtles** and several species of migratory birds.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• During the 1960s and 1970s, the indigenous population of the Chagos Archipelago, known as the **Chagossians**, was forcibly removed to establish military facilities on Diego Garcia.
 
• The displacement of the Chagossians remains a deeply controversial issue, with ongoing legal and diplomatic efforts to address their rights.
 
 
 
• **Indian Ocean:**
 
 
• The Indian Ocean is the **third-largest ocean** in the world, covering about **20% of the Earth's water surface**.
 
• It is bounded by **Asia** to the north, **Africa** to the west, **Australia** to the east, and the **Southern Ocean** to the south.
 
• The ocean plays a significant role in global trade and climate regulation.
 
 
 
• **Other Oceanic Options:**
 
 
• **Arctic Ocean:** The smallest and shallowest of the world's oceans, located near the North Pole.
 
• **Atlantic Ocean:** The second-largest ocean, separating the Americas from Europe and Africa.
 
• **Pacific Ocean:** The largest and deepest ocean, stretching between the Americas to the east and Asia and Australia to the west.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a scalar quantity?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Temperature**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Scalar quantities** are physical quantities that are described by their magnitude alone and do not have a direction associated with them.

• **Temperature** is a scalar quantity because it is defined only by its magnitude (e.g., degrees Celsius or Kelvin) and does not involve any direction.

• Other scalar quantities include **mass, distance, speed, time, energy, and pressure**, which are specified by their magnitude without any directional component.

• In contrast, quantities like velocity, acceleration, and force are **vector quantities**, as they require both magnitude and direction for complete description. *Hence, temperature is the correct answer.*

• It is important to note that scalar quantities can be added, subtracted, multiplied, or divided using simple arithmetic operations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Vector quantities:** 

• **Velocity** is a vector quantity because it describes both the speed and the direction of an object's motion.

• **Acceleration** is a vector quantity that measures the rate of change of velocity and includes direction.

• **Force** is a vector quantity defined by both its magnitude and the direction in which it is applied.

• Examples of vector quantities include **displacement, momentum, and electric field**.

• **Scalar vs. Vector Comparison:** 

• **Scalar quantities** involve only magnitude, whereas **vector quantities** require both magnitude and direction.

• Operations involving vector quantities often require vector algebra, such as dot product or cross product.

• **Applications of Scalar Quantities:** 

• **Temperature** is crucial in fields such as thermodynamics, climate studies, and material science.

• Other scalar quantities like energy and pressure are vital in engineering, physics, and everyday applications.

• **Examples of scalar quantities:** 

• **Mass:** Describes the amount of matter in an object.

• **Time:** Measures the duration of an event or process.

• **Speed:** Indicates how fast an object is moving without specifying direction.

• **Distance:** Represents the total path length traveled by an object.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **SI Unit of Temperature:** The standard unit is **Kelvin (K)**, but temperature can also be measured in **Celsius (°C)** or **Fahrenheit (°F)** depending on the context.

• **Absolute Zero:** In the Kelvin scale, **0 K** is the lowest possible temperature where molecular motion ceases.

• **Scalar Quantity Operations:** Scalars can be combined using basic arithmetic, unlike vectors, which require vector-specific operations.

• **Applications:** Temperature measurement is critical in processes like cooking, refrigeration, industrial manufacturing, and scientific experiments.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly defines 'Revenue Deficit' in a government budget?

options.text: Excess of total expenditure over total receipts
Excess of revenue expenditure over revenue receipts
Excess of capital expenditure over capital receipts
Excess of fiscal deficit over primary deficit

questions.solution:
**The correct answer is 'Excess of revenue expenditure over revenue receipts'**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

__
 
• **Revenue Deficit:**

 
 
• Revenue deficit refers to the shortfall in the government's revenue receipts compared to its revenue expenditure.
 
• It specifically indicates that the government is unable to meet its regular operational expenses from its revenue receipts and is relying on borrowing or other resources to cover these expenses.
 
• Revenue receipts include income from taxes (like income tax, GST, customs duty) and non-tax revenue (like interest receipts, dividends, and profits from public sector enterprises).
 
• Revenue expenditure includes spending on salaries, pensions, subsidies, interest payments, and other recurring expenses necessary for the functioning of the government.
 
• A revenue deficit highlights an imbalance in the government's finances and raises concerns about the sustainability of its fiscal practices.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Overview of Other Options:**

 
 
• **Excess of total expenditure over total receipts:**

 
 
• This is incorrect as it defines the **fiscal deficit**, not the revenue deficit.
 
• Fiscal deficit includes both revenue and capital accounts and represents the total borrowing requirement of the government.
 
 
 
• **Excess of capital expenditure over capital receipts:**
 
 
• This is incorrect as it refers to a specific imbalance in the capital account, but it is not the definition of revenue deficit.
 
• Capital expenditure includes spending on infrastructure, asset creation, and investments, while capital receipts include loans, disinvestment proceeds, and other non-recurring revenue sources.
 
 
 
• **Excess of fiscal deficit over primary deficit:**
 
 
• This is incorrect as it refers to the calculation of **interest payments** within the fiscal deficit framework.
 
• The primary deficit is the fiscal deficit minus interest payments, and this is not directly related to the concept of revenue deficit.
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• Revenue deficit is a crucial indicator of a government's fiscal health as it shows whether the government is able to meet its operational expenses without borrowing.
 
• A high revenue deficit can lead to increased borrowing, which in turn raises the fiscal deficit and debt burden.
 
• Reducing revenue deficit requires measures like increasing revenue receipts (e.g., better tax compliance, widening the tax base) and controlling revenue expenditure (e.g., reducing subsidies, improving efficiency in government spending).
 
• The concept of revenue deficit is unique to the revenue account and does not include capital receipts or capital expenditure.
 
• Persistent revenue deficits indicate structural issues in the economy that need to be addressed for long-term fiscal stability.

Match the following elements with their respective Atomicity
A. Monoatomic - a. Oxygen
B. Diatomic - b. Sulphur
C. Triatomic - c. Argon
D. Poly-atomic - d. Ozone
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A - Monoatomic (Argon), B - Diatomic (Oxygen), C - Triatomic (Ozone), D - Polyatomic (Sulphur)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Monoatomic elements**: Monoatomic substances are composed of single atoms. **Argon** is an example of a monoatomic gas as it exists as individual atoms in nature due to its inert properties.

• **Diatomic elements**: Diatomic molecules consist of two atoms of the same or different elements. **Oxygen (O₂)** is a diatomic molecule found naturally in the Earth's atmosphere.

• **Triatomic elements**: Triatomic molecules are composed of three atoms. **Ozone (O₃)** is a triatomic molecule formed naturally in the upper atmosphere, helping to block harmful ultraviolet radiation.

• **Polyatomic elements**: Polyatomic substances contain multiple atoms bonded together. **Sulphur** exists in a polyatomic form (e.g., S₈ in its solid state), forming cyclic or other molecular structures.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Monoatomic gases:** 

• **Noble gases** such as Argon, Helium, and Neon are examples of monoatomic substances because they do not readily form bonds due to their stable electronic configurations.

• These gases are commonly used in applications like lighting (e.g., neon lights), welding, and cooling systems.

• **Diatomic molecules:** 

• Examples include **Oxygen (O₂)**, Nitrogen (N₂), Hydrogen (H₂), and Halogens (e.g., Cl₂, F₂).

• Diatomic molecules are essential for life processes like respiration (oxygen) and industrial applications such as ammonia production (nitrogen).

• **Triatomic molecules:** 

• **Ozone (O₃)** is crucial for absorbing ultraviolet rays in the stratosphere.

• Triatomic molecules can also include water (H₂O), which plays a vital role in biological and chemical processes.

• **Polyatomic molecules:** 

• Examples include **Sulphur (S₈)**, Phosphorus (P₄), and Carbon-based molecules like glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆).

• Polyatomic molecules are essential in various industries, including agriculture, pharmaceuticals, and materials science.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Atomicity:** Atomicity refers to the number of atoms present in a molecule. For example, atomicity of Ozone is 3, Oxygen is 2, and Argon is 1.

• **Periodic table significance:** The classification of elements into monoatomic, diatomic, triatomic, and polyatomic forms is based on their bonding behavior and molecular structure.

• **Applications:** Understanding atomicity is crucial in chemistry for predicting reactivity, molecular behavior, and industrial applications.

 __ 
• **Statement 1:** The size of an object as perceived by the eye depends on its visual angle. 
• The visual angle is defined as the angle subtended by an object at the eye's lens. It depends on the object's size and distance from the observer. Objects closer to the eye appear larger, while objects farther away appear smaller. 
• This statement is **correct** as it aligns with the principles of optics and human visual perception. 
• **Statement 2:** The human eye is most sensitive to yellow-green light having a wavelength of 5550 Å (angstroms). 
• The peak sensitivity of the human eye lies in the yellow-green region of the visible spectrum, specifically around 555 nanometers (5550 Å), under daylight conditions (photopic vision). 
• This is due to the maximum response of cone cells in the retina to light in this wavelength range. 
• This statement is also **correct** based on human physiology and photometry. 
• **Correct Option:** Since both statements are correct, the option **Neither 1 nor 2**__ is the appropriate answer.

• The concept of visual angle is critical in understanding how the human eye perceives size and distance. 
• It is calculated using the formula: **Visual Angle = 2 × arctan(Object Size / (2 × Distance))**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Radiotherapy to treat cancer:

 
 
• High doses of radiation are used in radiation therapy, also known as radiotherapy, as a cancer treatment to eradicate cancer cells and reduce tumour size.
 
• As with x-rays of your teeth or shattered bones, radiation is utilised at low doses in x-rays to see inside your body.
 
• Radiation therapy damages cancer cells' DNA, which either kills them or limits their growth at high dosages.
 
• Cancer cells that have DNA damage that cannot be repaired either cease proliferating or die.
 
• When the injured cells expire, the body degrades and eliminates them.
 
• But too much radiation can damage tissues by changing cell structure and damaging DNA. This can cause serious health problems.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Surgery:

 
 
• Surgery is a medical speciality that employs operative manual and instrumental techniques on a patient to examine or treat a pathological condition.
 
• Such as a disease or injury, to enhance bodily function or appearance, or to repair unwelcome ruptured areas.
 
 
 
• Chemotherapy ​

questions.question: Which layer of Earth is responsible for plate movement through convection currents?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mantle**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **mantle** is the layer of the Earth located between the **crust** and the **core**. It extends from about 35 km below the Earth's surface to a depth of approximately 2,900 km.
 
• Plate movement is driven by **convection currents** in the mantle. These currents are caused by the transfer of heat from the Earth's core to its surface, resulting in the slow movement of semi-solid mantle material.
 
• The mantle is composed of **silicate rocks** rich in magnesium and iron, and it behaves as a **viscous fluid** over geological timescales.
 
• Convection currents in the mantle are responsible for the **movement of tectonic plates**, leading to phenomena such as **earthquakes**, **volcanism**, and the formation of **mountain ranges**.
 
• Hot material rises from the deeper mantle towards the surface, cools, and then sinks back, creating a continuous cycle that drives the **lithospheric plates** on the Earth's surface. *Hence, the mantle is responsible for plate movement.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Earth’s Layers:**

 
 
• The Earth is divided into four main layers: the **crust**, **mantle**, **outer core**, and **inner core**.
 
• The **crust** is the outermost layer, composed of solid rocks and minerals. It is where tectonic plates are located.
 
• The **outer core** is a layer of molten iron and nickel, while the **inner core** is solid due to immense pressure.
 
 
 
• **Convection Currents:**
 
 
• Convection currents are the result of **heat transfer** within the mantle. Heat from the core causes mantle materials to rise, cool, and sink in a cyclical pattern.
 
• This process is responsible for the **slow but continuous movement** of tectonic plates.
 
 
 
• **Plate Tectonics:**
 
 
• The movement of plates is explained by the **Plate Tectonic Theory**, which states that the Earth’s lithosphere is divided into plates that float on the semi-fluid mantle.
 
• This movement causes geological activities such as the formation of **mid-ocean ridges**, **subduction zones**, and **rift valleys**.
 
 
 
• **Role of Mantle in Plate Movement:**
 
 
• The mantle’s semi-solid state allows it to flow, albeit very slowly, providing the necessary force to move tectonic plates.
 
• Regions of rising mantle material are associated with **divergent boundaries**, while sinking material is linked to **convergent boundaries**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Crust:** The outermost layer; it is solid and forms the Earth’s surface. It does not contribute directly to convection currents.
 
• **Outer Core:** The liquid layer composed of iron and nickel, responsible for generating the Earth’s **magnetic field**, but it does not cause plate movement.
 
• **Inner Core:** The solid innermost layer of the Earth, it remains static and does not participate in convection currents.
 
• **Evidence of Mantle Dynamics:** Phenomena like **volcanoes**, **earthquakes**, and the **movement of continents** are direct consequences of mantle convection.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both (i) and (ii)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The relative strength of the magnetic field:** The closeness of magnetic field lines represents the relative strength of the magnetic field. The closer the lines, the stronger the magnetic field in that region. This is a fundamental property of magnetic field lines. ***Hence, statement (i) is correct.***
 
• **Intersection of magnetic field lines:** Magnetic field lines never intersect each other. If they did, it would mean that at the point of intersection, the magnetic field has two different directions, which is physically impossible. ***Hence, statement (ii) is correct.***
 
• **Magnetic field around a bar magnet:** The magnetic field lines emerge from the north pole of the bar magnet and enter the south pole, forming closed loops. This pattern demonstrates the continuous nature of magnetic field lines.
 
• **Representation of field strength:** The density of field lines (lines per unit area) around a bar magnet visually indicates the intensity of the magnetic field in a particular region.
 
• **Applications:** Understanding magnetic field lines is crucial in various applications such as designing magnets, electric motors, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Magnetic field lines:**

 
 
• Magnetic field lines are imaginary lines that represent the direction and strength of a magnetic field.
 
• They are denser near the poles of a magnet, indicating stronger magnetic fields in these areas.
 
• The field lines are continuous loops that extend from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet and from the south pole to the north pole inside the magnet.
 
 
 
• **Magnetic field properties:**
 
 
• The magnetic field is a vector quantity, having both magnitude and direction.
 
• The strength of the magnetic field decreases as the distance from the magnet increases.
 
 
 
• **Applications of magnetic fields:**
 
 
• Magnetic fields are used in various devices such as electric motors, generators, transformers, and magnetic storage devices.
 
• They are also used in medical imaging techniques such as MRI.
 
 
 
• **Earth's magnetic field:**
 
 
• The Earth behaves like a giant bar magnet with its magnetic field lines extending from the magnetic south pole to the magnetic north pole.
 
• It protects the Earth from harmful solar radiation by deflecting charged particles.
 
 
 
• **Magnetic field visualization:**
 
 
• Iron filings can be used to visualize magnetic field lines. When placed near a magnet, the filings align themselves along the field lines.
 
• This experiment helps in understanding the pattern and distribution of magnetic fields around a magnet.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Magnetic monopoles:** Unlike electric charges, magnetic monopoles do not exist. Every magnet has both a north and a south pole.
 
• **Magnetism in materials:** Materials can be classified as diamagnetic, paramagnetic, or ferromagnetic based on their response to magnetic fields.
 
• **Historical significance:** The study of magnets dates back to ancient Greece, where naturally occurring magnets were first discovered in the region of Magnesia.
 
• **Modern advancements:** Magnetic materials are used in advanced technologies such as maglev trains, data storage devices, and magnetic levitation systems.

• **Enfield Rifle Incident:** 
 

• The introduction of the **Enfield rifle** required soldiers to bite off the cartridge before loading, which was greased with animal fat. 

• This was offensive to both **Hindus** (cow fat) and **Muslims** (pig fat), causing widespread resentment and refusal to use the rifle. 

• The cartridge issue symbolized the disrespect of British authorities towards Indian religious and cultural sensitivities. 
 
 

• **Social and Political Causes:** 
 

• Beyond the cartridge issue, the revolt was fueled by various factors, including **economic exploitation**, **land reforms**, and **racial discrimination**. 

• The **Doctrine of Lapse**, introduced by Lord Dalhousie, was another major grievance. It deprived Indian rulers of their states if they lacked a male heir. 

• Excessive taxation policies and the destruction of traditional industries also contributed to widespread discontent. 
 
 

• **Outcome of the Revolt:** 
 

• Although the revolt was suppressed, it marked the beginning of the end of the **East India Company’s rule**. Power was transferred to the British Crown through the **Government of India Act, 1858**. 

• The revolt led to significant changes in British policies, including increased sensitivity to Indian cultural and religious issues. 

• It also sowed the seeds of nationalism, eventually leading to the **Indian independence movement** in the 20th century. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Timeline:** The revolt began on **10 May 1857** in Meerut and lasted till **1858**. 

• **Role of Sepoys:** Indian soldiers, or sepoys, played a crucial role in initiating the revolt, highlighting their dissatisfaction with British policies. 

• **Religious Sensitivities:** Disrespect towards religious beliefs, such as the cartridge issue, fueled anger among Indian communities. 

• **British Suppression:** The British used advanced weaponry and reinforcements to suppress the revolt, leading to immense casualties and destruction. 

• **Significance:** The revolt highlighted the need for organized resistance against colonial rule and marked the beginning of Indian nationalism.

questions.question: Which of the following monetary control tools refer to the buying and selling of bonds issued by the Government?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Open Market Operation**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Open Market Operation (OMO)** refers to the **buying and selling of government bonds and securities** by a central bank (e.g., the Reserve Bank of India - RBI) in the open market. 
• OMOs are conducted to regulate the **money supply and liquidity** in the economy, ensuring price stability and growth. 
• When the central bank **buys government bonds**, it injects liquidity into the economy by increasing the money supply, which is often done during periods of economic slowdown. 
• Conversely, when the central bank **sells government bonds**, it absorbs excess liquidity from the market, helping control inflation during periods of economic overheating. 
• OMOs play a crucial role in implementing the **monetary policy** of a country, aimed at achieving macroeconomic objectives such as controlling inflation, stabilizing the currency, and fostering economic growth. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF):** 
• LAF is a monetary policy tool used by the RBI to **manage liquidity** in the economy and control short-term interest rates. 
• It comprises **repo and reverse repo operations**, where banks borrow or lend funds to the RBI against collateral. 
• This tool is used to address short-term liquidity mismatches in the banking system. 
• **Bank Rate:** 
• The bank rate is the **interest rate** at which the RBI lends funds to commercial banks without requiring any collateral. 
• It is a long-term rate used to influence credit availability and regulate inflation or deflation. 
• An increase in the bank rate discourages borrowing and helps control inflation, while a decrease has the opposite effect. 
• **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF):** 
• MSF is a facility provided by the RBI that allows banks to borrow overnight funds at a rate higher than the repo rate. 
• It is intended to provide **emergency liquidity** to banks in times of severe cash shortages. 
• The MSF rate is usually set above the repo rate, encouraging banks to manage liquidity efficiently. 
• **Additional Facts About Open Market Operation:** 
• OMOs are conducted by the RBI through auctions using an electronic trading platform called **Negotiated Dealing System-Order Matching (NDS-OM).** 
• During the COVID-19 pandemic, the RBI conducted special OMOs, also known as "Operation Twist," to manage the yield curve effectively. 
• OMOs are considered a crucial component of **quantitative easing** in advanced economies, such as the United States and the European Union. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Key Differences Between Repo Rate and OMO:** 
• **Repo Rate:** A short-term tool where banks borrow funds from the RBI by selling securities with an agreement to repurchase them later. 
• **OMO:** A broader tool involving the outright purchase or sale of government bonds to manage the money supply. 
• **Role of OMOs in Indian Context:** 
• The RBI primarily uses OMOs to stabilize the rupee, manage inflation, and ensure adequate liquidity in the economy. 
• During periods of economic stress, OMOs help in easing borrowing costs for businesses and consumers. </ul

questions.question: Which government initiative focuses on cleaning rivers in India?
questions.solution:
**The correct answer is 'Namami Gange Programme'**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

__
 
• **Namami Gange Programme:**
 
 
• The Namami Gange Programme is an integrated conservation mission launched by the Government of India in 2014 to clean and rejuvenate the Ganga River and its tributaries.
 
• It aims to address various issues such as pollution abatement, river surface cleaning, rural sanitation, afforestation, and biodiversity conservation.
 
• The programme is implemented by the National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG) and State Program Management Groups (SPMGs).
 
• It focuses on infrastructure development, such as sewage treatment plants, to prevent untreated wastewater from entering the river.
 
• The initiative also includes public awareness campaigns, community participation, and the promotion of sustainable agricultural practices in the Ganga basin.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Green Revolution:**
 
 
• The Green Revolution was a period of agricultural transformation in India during the 1960s and 70s that focused on increasing food grain production, particularly of wheat and rice, through high-yield variety seeds, irrigation, and chemical fertilizers.
 
• While it significantly enhanced food security in India, it is unrelated to river cleaning initiatives.
 
 
 
• **Swachh Bharat Mission:**
 
 
• Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM), launched in 2014, aims to achieve universal sanitation coverage and eliminate open defecation in India.
 
• The mission is focused on building household and community toilets and promoting hygiene practices but does not specifically target river cleaning.
 
 
 
• **Make in India:**
 
 
• Make in India is a government initiative launched in 2014 to encourage manufacturing and investment in India by creating a conducive environment for businesses.
 
• It focuses on industrial growth and economic development but has no direct connection to environmental or river-cleaning efforts.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The Namami Gange Programme is a flagship initiative under the Ministry of Jal Shakti and is supported by a budget of several thousand crores to ensure effective implementation.
 
• It aligns with international environmental goals and commitments, such as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly Goal 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation).
 
• The programme has seen significant milestones, including the commissioning of numerous sewage treatment plants and the reduction of industrial effluents discharged into the Ganga River.
 
• It emphasizes the participation of local communities, NGOs, and other stakeholders to ensure its long-term sustainability and success.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the aftermath of the 1857 Revolt:

 
• The Indian Council Act of 1858 introduced the "Portfolio System" to the Governor-General’s Executive Council.
 
• The Act of 1858 stated that the British Crown would no longer annex any further Indian territories.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **__Only 2__**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Portfolio System** in the Governor-General’s Executive Council was **formally introduced by Lord Canning in 1859** and later **legalized by the Indian Councils Act, 1861**, not by the **Indian Council Act of 1858**.
 
• The **, also known as the Act for the Better Government of India, marked the transfer of power from the East India Company to the British Crown**. This act explicitly stated that the Crown would no longer annex further Indian territories, aiming to stabilize governance post-1857 Revolt. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• Both measures were introduced as significant administrative and political responses to the **1857 Revolt**, focusing on better governance and addressing the grievances of Indian society.
 
• The revolt exposed the weaknesses of the East India Company's administration, leading to reforms such as the introduction of direct British Crown rule in India.
 
• **The Portfolio System** was a step toward decentralizing governance, allowing for more efficient management of specific administrative functions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Indian Council Act of 1858:**

 
 
• The act abolished the East India Company and transferred power directly to the British Crown, marking the beginning of direct British rule in India.
 
• The Governor-General was made the representative of the Crown, with the title changed to **Viceroy of India**.
 
• It introduced reforms in administration, such as the creation of the Council of India to assist the Secretary of State for India.
 
• The act aimed to address administrative inefficiency and discontent that led to the 1857 Revolt.
 
 
 
• **Effects of the 1857 Revolt:**
 
 
• The revolt led to the end of the East India Company’s rule and the establishment of British Crown rule over India.
 
• It brought significant military reforms to prevent future uprisings, such as increasing the ratio of British to Indian soldiers.
 
• Policies like non-annexation and respect for Indian princely states were adopted to placate Indian rulers and elites.
 
• The British administration introduced measures to address the grievances of Indian society, including reforms in land revenue policies and governance.
 
 
 
• **Portfolio System:**
 
 
• This system divided the responsibilities of governance among members of the Governor-General’s Executive Council.
 
• Each member was assigned a specific portfolio such as finance, home affairs, or defense to manage independently.
 
• This was a move toward decentralization and more efficient governance.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Act of 1858:**
 
 
• The act marked a shift in governance, with the British Crown taking direct control of Indian administration.
 
• It addressed the administrative inefficiencies that contributed to the revolt and aimed to strengthen British control in India.
 
• The act laid the foundation for subsequent administrative reforms and policies in British India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **1857 Revolt:**

 
 
• Also known as the **First War of Indian Independence**, it was a major uprising against British rule in India.
 
• Causes included policies like the **Doctrine of Lapse**, economic exploitation, and socio-religious interference.
 
• Military grievances such as the use of animal fat in cartridges and unequal treatment of Indian soldiers were major triggers.
 
• The revolt spread across northern and central India but failed due to lack of coordination and support from all sections of society.
 
 
 
• **Administrative Reforms Post-1857:**
 
 
• Reforms focused on stabilizing governance and addressing Indian grievances to prevent further uprisings.
 
• The British increased the ratio of British troops to Indian troops and placed key military positions under British control.
 
• Policies like respect for Indian customs and non-annexation were introduced to placate Indian rulers and elites.
 
• Efforts were made to involve Indians in governance, such as through the Indian Councils Act of 1861.

questions.question: Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) operate at which level?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Village level**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) operate at the **village level**, serving as the lowest tier of the cooperative credit structure in India.
 
• PACS are formed by local farmers and rural residents to provide **short-term and medium-term loans** to support agricultural and rural development.
 
• They facilitate credit access for small and marginal farmers, ensuring timely availability of agricultural inputs such as seeds, fertilizers, and equipment.
 
• PACS also function as a link between rural borrowers and higher-tier institutions like District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs).
 
• They are pivotal in promoting financial inclusion in rural areas, addressing the credit needs of the unorganized agricultural sector.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **State Level**:
 
 
• At the state level, cooperative banks operate as apex institutions, such as State Cooperative Banks (SCBs).
 
• SCBs coordinate and supervise the functioning of District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and provide financial support to them.
 
• They play a vital role in implementing government policies related to rural credit and development.
 
 
 
• **Taluka Level**:
 
 
• There is no direct operation of PACS at the taluka level, but cooperative societies may indirectly interact with administrative units at this level.
 
• Taluka-level organizations may assist in monitoring and guiding PACS in their jurisdiction.
 
 
 
• **District Level**:
 
 
• District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) operate at the district level as intermediaries between PACS and State Cooperative Banks.
 
• DCCBs provide funding to PACS and ensure the smooth flow of credit to rural areas.
 
• They also help in implementing banking and credit policies for agricultural development in their respective districts.
 
 
 
• **About Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS)**:
 
 
• PACS are registered cooperative societies that form the foundation of the rural cooperative credit system in India.
 
• They are owned and controlled by members, who are typically local farmers and rural residents.
 
• PACS also perform additional functions such as distributing fertilizers, seeds, and other agricultural inputs, along with marketing agricultural produce.
 
• They play a critical role in ensuring rural credit delivery and enhancing the socio-economic conditions of rural communities.

questions.question: During Alauddin Khalji's reign, which general led the significant invasions of South India (Deccan)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Malik Kafur**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Malik Kafur was a prominent general during the reign of Alauddin Khalji, the Sultan of Delhi, and played a key role in expanding the Sultanate's territories.
 
• He led successful military expeditions to South India (Deccan) between 1309 and 1311, conquering kingdoms such as the Yadavas of Devagiri, the Kakatiyas of Warangal, the Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra, and the Pandyas of Madurai.
 
• Malik Kafur's invasions brought immense wealth to the Delhi Sultanate, including precious jewels, gold, and other riches from South Indian temples and royal treasuries.
 
• He was a trusted lieutenant of Alauddin Khalji, known for his military acumen and loyalty, which earned him the title "Hazardinari" as he was initially purchased as a slave for 1,000 dinars.
 
• Malik Kafur's campaigns marked the northern expansion into the Deccan and contributed significantly to Alauddin Khalji's ambition of consolidating his empire.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Nusrat Khan**

 
 
• Nusrat Khan was another prominent general under Alauddin Khalji and played a key role in the early military campaigns of the Delhi Sultanate.
 
• He was instrumental in the conquest of Gujarat in 1299 and the suppression of rebellions in northern India during Alauddin's reign.
 
• However, Nusrat Khan was not associated with the Deccan campaigns led by Malik Kafur.
 
 
 
• **Ain-ul-Mulk Multani**
 
 
• Ain-ul-Mulk Multani was a noble and governor under Alauddin Khalji who was entrusted with administrative duties and military expeditions.
 
• He was primarily involved in campaigns against Rajput rulers and rebellions in northern India, such as the suppression of the revolt in Gujarat.
 
• He did not lead the invasions of South India.
 
 
 
• **Ghazi Malik**
 
 
• Ghazi Malik, later known as Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, was a governor under Alauddin Khalji and eventually the founder of the Tughlaq dynasty.
 
• He was known for his military campaigns in the north-western regions of India but had no direct involvement in the Deccan invasions.
 
 
 
• **Overview of Alauddin Khalji's Deccan Campaigns**
 
 
• The Deccan campaigns were a significant milestone in the history of the Delhi Sultanate, marking the first major incursions into South India.
 
• Alauddin Khalji's ambition to control the wealth and resources of the Deccan led to these expeditions under the leadership of Malik Kafur.
 
• The campaigns demonstrated the military superiority of the Sultanate while showcasing the strategic importance of South India in medieval Indian history.
